Build a rerunnable experiment pipeline

Why: The lasting value of shell scripting is making a useful experiment repeatable after weeks or years away.

A rerunnable pipeline has a defined input set, known tools, an explicit order, and a clear output contract. Begin with one file and one analysis command. Add validation and a small test fixture before scaling to a folder. The top-level script should read like a short explanation of the workflow rather than a puzzle of nested one-liners.

Choose what happens on rerun. A unique per-run output directory avoids confusing old results with new ones. A deliberate overwrite policy can also work for generated artifacts, but it must never target the raw observations. Record arguments, code revision, relevant versions, and input identity. A checksum helps distinguish changed bytes; it is not a statement about scientific quality.

At the end, verify the expected outputs rather than merely reaching the final line. Did every selected input get an outcome? Is the result parseable, nonempty when required, and associated with the current run? Write a short limitations note. Your first pipeline might summarize invented rover logs; later the same structure can coordinate MATLAB models, Python analysis, and simulator outputs without hiding their assumptions.

Worked example

#!/usr/bin/env bash
if [[ $# -ne 1 || ! -r "$1" ]]; then
  printf "Usage: summarize READABLE_LOG\n" >&2
  exit 2
fi
printf "Input: %s\n" "$1"
if wc -l < "$1"; then
  printf "Line-count step completed\n" >&2
else
  printf "Line-count step failed\n" >&2
  exit 1
fi

This is a deliberately small starting pipeline. Expand it only after defining and testing each additional boundary.

Your workflow

  • Write the workflow contract in a README.
  • Validate before running analysis.
  • Record a per-run manifest and keep raw data unchanged.
  • Verify outputs and report both successes and failures.

Common traps

  • Reusing a stale output after a failed run.
  • Declaring success because the script reached its end.
  • Growing a shell script into an undocumented data-processing language.

Start · Workflow contract

Write the input, output, success, and failure contract for a log-summary script.

Input: One newline-terminated text log.

Expected: A reader knows what counts are produced and what invalid input does.

Hints & worked reasoning
  • Specify the format, not just the filename.
  • Name the expected error outcomes.

Document required file readability, severity-line format, count outputs, status codes, and preservation of the source log.

Test cases

  • An empty input has a defined meaning.
  • A missing input has a different outcome.

Extend: Add an example fixture and expected summary.

Build · Fresh outputs

Design a per-run output directory policy that prevents old results from masquerading as current results.

Input: Two executions with different input logs.

Expected: Each run has a distinct identifiable result set.

Hints & worked reasoning
  • Use a run identifier.
  • Validate the target before creating results.

Require a new run directory or reject an existing one under the chosen policy. Store a manifest alongside generated artifacts.

Test cases

  • The second run cannot silently read the first summary.
  • Raw inputs remain outside the generated output folder.

Extend: Add a human-readable summary of the run.

Stretch · Cross-language orchestration

Plan Bash validation followed by Python analysis and MATLAB comparison, using CSV as an explicit interface.

Input: Shared columns time_s and temperature_c.

Expected: Each stage has a documented format, status check, and evidence artifact.

Hints & worked reasoning
  • Bash coordinates; numerical code analyzes.
  • Check the producer before invoking its consumer.

Validate filenames and tool availability, run the producer, inspect its status, validate the output schema, then run the comparison. Record versions and assumptions.

Test cases

  • Failed analysis prevents comparison.
  • A schema mismatch is reported explicitly.

Extend: Add a small end-to-end fixture with a known answer.

Debug · Stale success artifact

A script reads summary.csv after analysis fails; the file was left by yesterday’s run. Why is existence checking insufficient?

Input: An old valid-looking summary remains.

Expected: Associate outputs with the current successful run.

Hints & worked reasoning
  • Status and provenance both matter.
  • Use fresh output locations.

Stop on analysis failure and use a new run directory or a verified current-run marker. A stale file should never satisfy the new run’s success contract.

Test cases

  • A failing run cannot publish yesterday’s result.
  • The manifest identifies the current inputs.

Extend: Test this case deliberately in a scratch directory.

Recall

What makes a pipeline rerunnable?

Explicit inputs and environment, controlled output policy, checked dependencies, and enough provenance to reproduce the result.

When should a shell pipeline call another language?

When structured parsing, numerical analysis, complex data models, or detailed testing is clearer in a dedicated programming language.

The rover mass and energy ledger

Build a small command-line engineering ledger that makes units, assumptions, and missing information visible. Start with invented component data, then use measured values from a harmless desktop build.

Define the component schema

A CSV containing component_id, mass_kg, average_power_w, and a note describing the power assumption.

Acceptance: Every row has a unique ID; masses and power values are finite and nonnegative; invalid rows receive explicit reasons.

Compute transparent totals

A summary with total mass, total assumed power, and ideal energy for a specified duration.

Acceptance: A hand-checked three-component fixture matches exactly or within documented floating-point tolerance. The ideal model is labeled.

Make the interface repeatable

A CLI accepting input, duration, and output path.

Acceptance: --help states units; changing duration does not require source edits; the input file remains unchanged.

Prepare a useful design review

A short report comparing two component selections and listing omitted effects.

Acceptance: The report distinguishes measured, manufacturer-stated, and assumed quantities and does not claim actual battery runtime from an ideal constant-power estimate.

Test plan

  • Zero components produces a documented empty-ledger response.
  • Duplicate component IDs are rejected.
  • A negative mass or non-finite power is reported.
  • Doubling duration doubles ideal energy without changing mass.

Portfolio evidence

  • README with the physical question and unit conventions.
  • Small fixture and tests.
  • One comparison report with assumptions and limitations.
  • A note explaining what real measurements would improve the estimate.

Constraints

  • No optimization claim without a defined objective and constraints.
  • No hardware purchase or physical robot is required.
  • Keep the model simple enough to verify by hand.

Verify the implementation

Acceptance: Solver success is checked and maximum difference from the exact solution is reported over the same times.

A calibration and residual workbench

Construct known data

A synthetic linear calibration dataset with documented slope, offset, units, and optional seeded noise.

Acceptance: An exact no-noise fixture recovers the known coefficients within numerical tolerance.

Fit and inspect

A least-squares fit, residual plot, and coefficient report with the fitted input interval.

Acceptance: Residual sign and loss definition are documented; the design matrix columns are explained.

Evaluate beyond the fitting rows

A held-out synthetic set or independent benign dataset, with an evaluation plan written first.

An offline robot inspection supervisor

Specify behavior

A transition table for waiting, ready, inspecting, and review_required, with explicit reset behavior.

Acceptance: Every documented state/event pair has a next state or an explicit ignored-event result.

Build a pure transition core

A function consuming state, event, and timing information and returning a new state plus explanation.

Acceptance: The function performs no sleeping, network calls, or physical I/O and can be tested with fixed values.

Acceptance: A written expected state trace is compared against the generated trace for each fixture.

  • Start is ignored while waiting.

  • A short failure analysis for one stale-data scenario.

A reproducible engineering study runner

Build a general but small experiment runner that varies parameters, validates each case, records provenance, and compares results across runs.

Choose a benign model

A documented algebraic or thermal model with known units, input domain, and at least one exact reference case.

Acceptance: The model can be independently checked; no operational propulsion or weapon-design parameters are required.

Define a study configuration

A JSON file listing parameter cases, output location, and model version label.

Acceptance: Invalid cases are rejected with reasons; case identifiers are unique and deterministic.

Run and record

A runner producing per-case result records and a manifest with configuration and input identifiers.

Acceptance: A failed case does not masquerade as a successful zero; successful outputs retain their originating parameters.

Compare and communicate

A parameter-response plot and short report stating sensitivity, limitations, and the next measurement that would reduce uncertainty.

Acceptance: The entire study is recreated by one documented command and a tiny fixture passes in a clean environment.

Test plan

  • Use published or synthetic data whose units and provenance are known.
  • Do not generalize beyond the model’s stated domain.

  • Exact line recovery.
  • Input length and finite-value checks.
  • Held-out prediction remains independent of fitting.

Portfolio evidence

  • Calibration plot and residual plot.
  • A clear explanation of slope and offset.
  • An honest supported-range statement.

Constraints

  • Synthetic data must be labeled.
  • No claim of metrological certification.
  • Do not hide outliers solely to improve fit.

Synthetic vibration detective

Build a frequency-analysis notebook that correctly identifies known synthetic signals and explains when sampling makes identification impossible.

Generate known signals

One sinusoid and a two-component signal with recorded sample rates.

Acceptance: The sample-time vector and sample counts match the intended experiment.

Verify the spectrum

A correctly labeled frequency axis and documented scaling convention.

Acceptance: Known bin-centered peaks appear at the predicted frequencies.

Demonstrate ambiguity

An aliasing example with two distinct continuous frequencies producing matching samples.

Acceptance: The numerical comparison is tied to an algebraic explanation.

Write the interpretation

A report separating signal evidence from mechanical-cause speculation.

Acceptance: The limitations explain finite records, sampling, noise, and untested assumptions.

Test plan

  • A DC input peaks at zero frequency.
  • A bin-centered sinusoid gives the expected mirrored bins.
  • Frequency labels change correctly when Fs changes.

Portfolio evidence

  • A known-signal verification figure.
  • An aliasing demonstration.
  • A paragraph explaining what the spectrum cannot establish.

Constraints

  • Use synthetic or public data; no operating propulsion hardware is required.
  • A spectrum alone does not diagnose machinery health.
  • Check licenses for optional toolboxes.

Thermal design assumption explorer

Compare how a simplified enclosure model responds to parameter choices and present a trade study without turning assumptions into false certainty.

Choose a narrow question

A parameter table and a threshold question within the model’s domain.

Acceptance: Every varied quantity has units and an explicit plausible range or labeled illustrative range.

Sweep deterministically

A grid of model outputs with inputs stored alongside them.

Acceptance: A manually checked corner case matches the automated result.

Explore uncertainty

Optional seeded sampling plus a statement of distribution assumptions.

Acceptance: The same seed reproduces the experiment and probability claims remain conditional on the assumed distributions.

Make the decision visible

A trade plot, ranked sensitivities, and a recommendation for the next measurement.

Acceptance: The conclusion identifies which input uncertainty limits the result rather than claiming a certified design.

Test plan

  • Boundary cases obey model limits.
  • Seeded trials reproduce.
  • Threshold roots are checked by substitution.

Portfolio evidence

  • A trade-space visualization.
  • A reproducible experiment manifest.
  • A recommendation grounded in model limitations.

Constraints

  • Illustrative trade study only; no flight or habitat certification.
  • Do not interpret arbitrary parameter ranges as real probability distributions.
  • Keep numerical error separate from physical uncertainty.
